title: Choosing the pattern for the problem, not for your CV

videos.script: Eighteen lessons have given you a lot of patterns. This last one is about when not to use them. {{title}} A pattern is an answer. Chosen before the question, it is only a cost with a name on it. {{answer}} So the lesson starts with the question. What hurts, in one sentence? Something changes and the change is expensive, or a part knows what it should not. {{force}} Then you will count what a pattern costs. The same fine notice, written as one function and as six classes. A small program counts the calls a reader has to follow. One against nine. {{hops}} Another program reads your code and asks questions about it. A protocol with one implementation. A parameter nobody reads. {{smells}} Then three real decisions from the library, argued out loud. Each one names its force, rejects a bigger answer, and says what would reopen it. {{decisions}} You will read a file full of patterns with no names on them, and learn to tell them apart by what they hold. {{shapes}} And you will write the choice down, in a page short enough that somebody reads it. {{record}}
